drafts.question: What shell company red flags should a depository institution look for when the registration data on a business customer does not line up with its stated business - specifically around NAICS codes, addresses, name variations, and EINs?
drafts.summary:
The most directly on-point source is FinCEN's Advisory FIN-2019-A006 (fentanyl/synthetic opioids), which sets out a set of shell-company red flags for depository institutions organised exactly around the categories you ask about: industry/business-line discrepancy, company address or location discrepancy, company name discrepancy, and Employer Identification Number (EIN) discrepancy. One caveat: the retrieved text does not use the term "NAICS code" — the industry-discrepancy flag is framed as the company operating in a different industry than the business name indicates and being associated with multiple businesses in unrelated industries. FATF/Egmont TBML risk indicators supplement the address and name points.

Industry/business-line discrepancy: the company appears in a different industry than its name suggests; commercial databases link it to multiple businesses in unrelated industries; it has no website or only a vague one.

Address discrepancy: open-source searches on the provided address return a different business name, or an operating location inconsistent with the business model (e.g., a residence); commercial databases show multiple active addresses or operating locations without any indication of franchises, branches, subsidiaries or agents. FATF adds mass-registration addresses (PO boxes, high-density residential or commercial buildings with no unit number) and business activity that does not fit the stated address.

Name discrepancy: a vague, non-descriptive name that does not align with the business model; three or more name variations or multiple "doing business as" names in commercial databases. FATF also flags names that copy or closely resemble a well-known corporation.

EIN discrepancy: commercial databases show the company is a small business (fewer than 500 employees) yet holds multiple EINs or shares EINs with other businesses.

As FATF notes, a single indicator does not by itself warrant suspicion; institutions should weigh the totality of the customer profile, and several co-occurring indicators warrant closer examination.

claims.text: FinCEN Advisory FIN-2019-A006 lists shell-company red flags for depository institutions grouped as industry discrepancy, company address or location discrepancy, company name discrepancy, and Employer Identification Number (EIN) discrepancy.

An industry-discrepancy red flag is that the company appears to be in a different industry than the business name indicates, and that commercial databases associate the company with multiple businesses in unrelated industries.
Open source information showing that the company lacks a website or has only a vague company website is a shell-company red flag.

An address red flag is that online or other open-source searches on the address provided reveal a business with a different name, or an operating location inconsistent with the business model, such as a residence.

Another address red flag is that commercial databases associate the company with multiple active addresses or operating locations while revealing few if any indications the company has franchises, multiple branches, subsidiaries or agents.
A name red flag is that the company's name is vague, non-descriptive, or does not align with its business model.
A further name red flag is that commercial databases reveal the company has three or more name variations or multiple 'doing business as' (dba) names.
The EIN red flag is that commercial databases reveal the company is a small business with fewer than 500 employees but has multiple EINs or shares EINs with other businesses.

FATF/Egmont TBML risk indicators include an entity being registered at a likely mass-registration address, such as high-density residential buildings, post-box addresses, commercial buildings or industrial complexes, especially with no reference to a specific unit.
FATF/Egmont also flag business activity that does not appear appropriate for the stated address, such as an entity using residential property without a commercial premises.
FATF/Egmont flag an entity name that copies or closely resembles the name of a well-known corporation, potentially to appear part of that corporation.
FATF/Egmont flag trade or business activity that is inconsistent with the stated line of business of the entities involved, for example a car dealer exporting clothing.

FATF guidance states that the existence of a single indicator may not alone warrant suspicion, but could prompt further monitoring, and that several co-occurring indicators warrant closer examination, taking into account the totality of the customer profile.

The FATF Comprehensive Update on Terrorist Financing Risks similarly lists a company address inconsistent with the business in which it is engaged, a company lacking online presence or having an online presence inconsistent with its purported activities, and a company name that mimics more-established competitors.
